messages.subject: Same animals observed in different areas that overlaped
messages.subject_clean: Same animals observed in different areas that overlaped
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a question about how I should use point trensect data, I have point transect observations where an observer count the individuals in one area and then move to the another one, stop to the second area once the observer arrive and count the animals they see.
The point is that in some occasions, the areas are very close to each other, and the observer knows that some animals that they recorded in the previous area are now in the second area that they count. How can I treat those "duplicates"? Should I remove it? Or Would I consider different observations in a different area? Because I am interested in knowing the total abundance (that could be overestimated if I consider the duplicates individuals), but as well I am interested in the abundance of individuals by areas.

Thank you in advance

Andreu

messages.body_plain:
Andreu

I think I understand your question; animals move from one point transect station to the adjacent station and are detected by the observer at each station.

If the observer can be certain the same individual is being detected, then excluding the second detection is a good idea.  I would suspect this is an infrequent event, do you know the frequency of this event? If it is infrequent, its effect upon your estimates is likely to be small.  Buckland (2006) showed by simulation that overlapping point transect sampling locations has a negligible effect upon density estimates:
Buckland, S. T. (2006). Point transect surveys for songbirds: Robust methodologies. The Auk, 123(2), 345–357. https://doi.org/10.1093/auk/123.2.345

When you say "abundance by area", what do you mean? Abundance by sampling station?

messages.body_plain:
Eric, Andreu,

I believe I asked the list a similar question once about line transects, but I cannot find it. My question was: on closely spaced transects, if an animal is first spotted on transect A and then moves to transect B where it is spotted again, should it be counted again? I forget who answered---Tiago Marques perhaps---and they said yes, it should be counted again. They pointed out that so long as the layout and execution of the transects are random with respect to animal movements, then for every animal that moved from transect A to B and was counted twice, there was, in principle, another animal that moved from B to A and was not counted on either transect. Thus, these missed animals would balance out the double-counted animals. I inferred from this that if the double-counted animals were only counted a single time, abundance would be underestimated.

Does that situation apply here?

Best regards,

Jason

messages.subject: mrds and Distance CRAN release
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance list,

We are pleased to announce the release of `mrds 2.3.0` and `Distance 1.0.9` on CRAN. An important update is that the default encounter rate variance estimator for point transect surveys has now been changed from the 'P3' estimator to the 'P2' estimator.

Please note that this change will only make a difference to the variance estimate when there is variable survey effort (e.g. variable numbers of visits) between points, which is rare in practice. In the case that points are visited the same number of times these two estimators ('P2' and 'P3') are equivalent and there will be no difference in the variance estimates.

This change to the default encounter rate estimator was made for consistency with the line transect estimator, where the equivalent 'R2' estimator is the default, and also with Distance for Windows where 'R2' and 'P2' are the defaults for line and point transect surveys, respectively. 'R2' and 'P2' are both design-based variance estimators, while 'R3' and 'P3' are model-derived; the design-based line transect estimator was found to be superior when model assumptions fail (see Fewster et. al. 2009, for details).

These releases also address a number of reported issues within the packages. A full list of changes and updates can be found in the package NEWS files: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mrds/NEWS / https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Distance/NEWS

Thanks to those who have made feature requests or reported issues. If you do find any problems, or want to suggest a new feature, please feel free to raise an issue at either  https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/Distance/issues or https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/mrds/issues

Best wishes,
Laura

Dr. L Marshall

Distance Development Team

Centre for Research into Ecological & Environmental Modelling

University of St. Andrews

Tel: +44 (0)1334 461808

Any density estimate has an associated measure of uncertainty, probably a standard error. Given the pair of estimates and their standard errors, a statistical test can be conducted. In Buckland et al. We're looking for a post doctoral fellow to join our research group at WCS Canada/University of Victoria. messages.subject_clean: Introductory distance sampling workshop; registration now open
messages.body_plain:
Interactive introductory distance sampling training

The University of St Andrews has been training ecologists and statisticians in design and analysis of distance sampling studies for decades. Distance sampling methods are widely used in population assessment of many different taxonomic groups. Perhaps you've wanted to attend a previous workshop, but schedules conflicted with your field work. 👨‍🌾

We are offering the training workshop in 10 2.5-hour blocks in March 2024.  You will be invited to interact in short lectures on distance sampling principles. 👩‍🎓 Exercises analysing data sets in R will reinforce those principles and the lecturer will be available to assist during the practical session via screen sharing.  The session will conclude with a summary of the exercise and question/answer session for both lecture and exercise. 💻  You can participate in polls during the workshop to assess your comprehension of topics discussed. 🤔 In addition to questions at any time during the lectures and practicals, an optional additional half hour will be set aside each session for discussion of topics arising. 🗣

The workshop will be delivered using Zoom web conferencing software along with R-Studio "in the cloud".☁️ You will need (free) accounts for both pieces of software. I encourage you to experiment with Zoom (at https://zoom.us) and https://posit.cloud before the workshop begins. 👩‍💻  There will be an internet connection testing and general orientation session the week of 22-26 Feb 2024.

Important details

Workshop dates and time:  04-15 March 2024; 1400-1630 British Standard Time.
For the time of day in your time zone, consult  https://www.timeanddate.com/worldclock/fixedtime.html?msg=Introductory+distance+sampling+workshop&iso=20240304T14&p1=3853&ah=2&am=30🕰️
Registration deadline: 21 Feb 2024📅
Enrolment limit: 14
Cost: 225 British pounds 💵
What is included: Lectures, exercises, code, data all available online📃

Widening participation scholarship

One place will have the registration fee waived, for participants from under-represented groups.  Details of eligibility and application process at  http://workshops.distancesampling.org/widening-participation. Deadline for scholarship application for the March 2024 introductory workshop is 24 January 2024.

What they are saying

> I would like to say I really liked RStudio Cloud and it is working just fine and I am really enjoying using it as a student. I'm looking forward to using it as an instructor too. I really liked the first half of the course. I love distance sampling and I am enjoying every second of the course! The only thing I can say about this particular workshop is it deserves more time. -- Kaan Özgencil, PhD student, Department of Biological Sciences, Middle East Technical University, Ankara

Further details

http://workshops.distancesampling.org/intro-mar-2024.html

At the webpage above, you will find a link to the St Andrews online shop where payment is made.  After you registration, I will contact you with additional details regarding workshop electronic materials, etc.

Feel free to contact me with questions. Please share this announcement with interested colleagues 🏢.

Information regarding all distance sampling workshops can be found at

https://workshops.distancesampling.org

Eric Rexstad

Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling

University of St Andrews

Registered Charity in Scotland SC013532

messages.subject: Distance Sampling Simulations
messages.body_plain:
Hi! I've been working with distance sampling for a few years now and I just started playing around with data simulations. The package 'dsims' is great, but I'm running into come complications. I have a shapefile of a county (area = 2,620 km2) and another of 30 transects of varying lengths (total = 231,905m). I set N to about 30,000 because that would be an appropriate abundance based on a density of 12. Then I set the truncation to 150m and scale to 75 for a half normal detection function. Once I go run 'run.survey' and to sur...@dist.data it only comes back with anywhere from 30-100 observations and some of them have NA's for distances. I know this to be a relatively low number because when we do this survey in the field we see more than that many observations. Additionally, some observations are beyond the specified truncation distance. I am also confused as to what the arguments sampler and line.length might do. I want to simulate running each transect twice, but I cannot figure out how to do that.

Any help would be greatly appreciated!
Thanks,
Jake
